subject: Cognitive Science
title: Inversion
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Inversion.

hook.text: Charlie Munger's secret: instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure—then avoid it.

buildup.text: Inversion means flipping the problem around: instead of pursuing the goal, avoid what prevents it.

discovery.text: Mathematician Carl Jacobi used it constantly: "Invert, always invert." Some problems only yield backward.

twist.text: It works because blind spots hide in forward thinking. Looking backward reveals obstacles you'd miss.

climax.text: Want a great relationship? List what destroys one—then systematically don't do those things.

punchline.text: To find the path forward, look backward.

quiz.question: What is the inversion mental model?
options: Approaching problems by considering what to avoid

details.summary: Inversion means approaching a problem backward by asking what you want to avoid rather than what you want to achieve. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how to fail, then avoid those paths. Carl Jacobi's advice to always invert reveals hidden obstacles and simplifies complex decisions.
details.whyItMatters: Inversion exposes risks and failure modes that forward thinking misses. It is often easier to identify what causes failure than what guarantees success.
takeaways: Think backward: identify what to avoid, not just what to pursue
Inversion reveals hidden risks and failure modes
Avoiding stupidity is often easier than seeking brilliance

faq.question: How do you apply inversion to everyday decisions?
faq.answer: Ask what would guarantee failure in your situation, then systematically avoid those things. For a project, list every way it could fail: missed deadlines, unclear goals, poor communication. Then design your process to prevent each failure mode.

faq.question: What is a famous example of inversion thinking?
faq.answer: Munger often said instead of asking how to be happy, ask what makes people miserable, then avoid those things: envy, resentment, unreliable behavior, and addiction. By systematically avoiding known causes of misery, happiness becomes more likely.
